text: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is an algorithmic rank aggregation method that combines ranked lists from multiple retrieval systems without needing score normalization. For each document d, its RRF score is computed as score(d) = sum_{m in M} 1 / (k + rank_m(d)), where M is the set of retrievers, rank_m(d) is the 1-indexed rank of document d in retriever m, and k is a smoothing constant typically set to 60. RRF effectively balances top candidates from both sparse (BM25) and dense (vector) retrieval.

metadata.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion in Information Retrieval

text: In hybrid retrieval pipelines, Reciprocal Rank Fusion is frequently deployed as the fusion layer. It merges sparse keyword candidates with dense semantic candidates to produce a single unified ranking. By taking the ranking positions from both retrievers, it helps surface relevant results even when raw retrieval scores operate on completely different scales.

BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a probabilistic sparse retrieval algorithm based on term frequency and inverse document frequency. Its scoring function incorporates document length normalization controlled by hyperparameter b (default 0.75) and term frequency saturation controlled by hyperparameter k1 (default 1.2 to 2.0). Higher k1 values allow repeated terms to contribute more to the score, whereas b penalizes excessively long documents.

Dense vector retrieval maps textual queries and passages into high-dimensional latent space using transformer encoder models like all-MiniLM-L6-v2. When embeddings are L2-normalized, the cosine similarity between two vectors is mathematically identical to their inner product (dot product). This allows fast maximum inner product search (MIPS) using FAISS IndexFlatIP without expensive square root distance computations.

metadata.title: Vector Embeddings and Inner Product Search

text: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) offers multiple vector index implementations. IndexFlatIP provides exact brute-force search with 100% recall but scales linearly O(N) in search latency. For million-scale datasets, Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes such as IndexIVFFlat (inverted file with Voronoi cells) or IndexHNSWFlat (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs) provide sub-linear search time at the cost of a slight recall tradeoff.

metadata.title: FAISS Index Selection and ANN Tradeoffs

text: Semantic- and Evidence-Aware Corrective RAG (CRAG) evaluates retrieved query-document candidates along two axes: Intent-Fit and Evidence-Sufficiency. Based on these two dimensions, the decision router chooses one of three actions: TRUST (evidence is relevant and sufficient), VERIFY-MORE (evidence is on-topic but incomplete, triggering supplementary retrieval), or REJECT-SEARCH (evidence is off-intent, triggering query rewriting and web fallback).

Query rewriting in commercial web search engines optimizes user input by expanding abbreviations, injecting domain synonyms, and correcting spelling errors. In contrast to database query planners, search rewrites focus on increasing recall across inverted document indexes by generating alternative lexical phrasing.

DeBERTa (Decoding-enhanced BERT with disentangled attention) improves upon BERT and RoBERTa by representing each token with two vectors: one encoding its semantic content and another encoding its relative position. Disentangled attention computes cross-attention scores across content-to-content, content-to-position, and position-to-content pairs, significantly improving performance on sequence classification and evaluator tasks.

The Raft consensus algorithm maintains state machine consistency across distributed server clusters. Raft decomposes consensus into three independent sub-problems: leader election, log replication, and commit safety. If a leader fails, follower nodes initiate a new election term using randomized election timeouts to prevent split votes.

Product Quantization (PQ) is a lossy compression technique used to reduce the memory footprint of vector databases. A high-dimensional vector of dimension D is divided into m smaller sub-vectors, and each sub-vector is quantized to its nearest centroid among a learned codebook. This compresses a 384-dimensional float32 vector (1536 bytes) into just a few dozen bytes, enabling billion-scale search on a single machine.
